overview:
Somewhere in the fourth millennium BCE, metalworkers in western Asia found that adding a small amount of tin to molten copper produced a metal harder, more castable and more durable than either parent — and archaeologists have used that discovery ever since to name a stretch of the human past. The label is a convenience rather than a date. Bronze working spread unevenly, so the period begins around 3300 BCE in Mesopotamia and Egypt, somewhat later in the Aegean and temperate Europe, and later still in Korea, where it starts closer to 1000 BCE; in China, where ritual bronze casting reached extraordinary sophistication under the Shang and Zhou, some scholars argue the Bronze Age never really ended so much as merged into later dynastic history. In the Americas, sub-Saharan Africa and Australia the framework simply does not fit, and archaeologists there use different periodisations entirely. What the term does capture is a genuine cluster of changes across Eurasia and North Africa: cities, hereditary kingship, written law, palace bureaucracies, and the world's first writing systems — cuneiform in Mesopotamia, hieroglyphs in Egypt, later the oracle-bone script in China and the undeciphered Indus signs.

The awkward fact at the centre of the age is that tin is rare. Copper is widely distributed; tin ore occurs in relatively few places, which meant that making bronze at scale required moving material across enormous distances, and that in turn required diplomacy, credit, shipping and record-keeping. The clearest single window onto this is the ship that sank off Uluburun on the Turkish coast around 1320 BCE, carrying roughly ten tonnes of Cypriot copper and a tonne of tin in exactly the ten-to-one ratio bronze demands, along with elephant tusks, ostrich eggshell, glass ingots, Baltic-style amber and a gold scarab bearing Nefertiti's name. Isotope work published in recent years traced part of that tin to the Taurus Mountains and part to Central Asia, in what is now Uzbekistan and Tajikistan — a supply chain reaching from the Hindu Kush to the Nile. Around this metal trade grew a genuinely international system: Egypt, the Hittites, Assyria, Babylonia, Mycenaean Greece and the Levantine port cities corresponded in Akkadian, exchanged gifts and brides, and fought over the same corridors.

That system came apart between roughly 1250 and 1150 BCE, in what is usually called the Late Bronze Age collapse. The Hittite empire dissolved, Ugarit burned, Mycenaean palace society vanished along with its Linear B administration, Cypriot and Levantine cities shrank, and Egypt survived only in reduced form. Why remains genuinely unsettled. Drought, earthquake sequences, internal revolt, epidemic disease, and the raiding groups Egyptian sources call the Sea Peoples have each been proposed as the trigger, and each explanation has holes; most historians now favour some version of Eric Cline's "perfect storm," in which several shocks arrived faster than any of these states could absorb them. In the eastern Mediterranean the following centuries are thinly documented, and the map's chosen endpoint of 599 BCE stretches the term well past the point where iron had become the ordinary working metal.
significance: Almost everything usually meant by "civilisation" in the Old World — the city, the state, the tax roll, the law code, the archive, the standing army, the long-distance market — first appears together in these millennia, and the tin trade in particular established that societies could become structurally dependent on materials from thousands of kilometres away. That dependency is also the period's most durable lesson: when the eastern Mediterranean's interlocking kingdoms fell in the twelfth century BCE, they fell largely together, and the collapse has become the standard case study for how tightly coupled systems fail. The written traditions that outlasted the wreckage — Homeric epic, the earliest layers of Hebrew scripture, Chinese dynastic memory — are in large part attempts by later people to explain a vanished bronze-age world to themselves.
coverage: This dataset currently holds no events beneath the Bronze Age, so the map can show nothing for a period spanning roughly 2,400 years and most of Eurasia and North Africa; the account above comes from general reference works and archaeological reporting rather than from anything the map can plot. The underlying record is also unevenly thin: absolute dates for the Aegean and Egypt are still disputed by a century or more, the Indus script is undeciphered, and the causes of the Late Bronze Age collapse remain openly contested, with much of the surviving testimony about the Sea Peoples coming from Egyptian royal inscriptions written to celebrate victory over them.
